items.title: Public Meeting to Consider A Zoning Amendment
Mayor Watters welcomed everyone and asked Council if there was any
notes: disclosure of Pecuniary Interest under the Municipal Conflict of Interest Act.

Mayor Watters stated the purpose of the public meeting is specific to the zoning amendment and is not intended to involve any information or discussions related to the licensing of Short Term Rental Accommodations.

He noted the purpose and effect of the proposed zoning by-law amendment is to modify the by-law provisions related to overnight accommodation, including hotels, motels, short-term rental accommodation, and bed and breakfast establishments.

He indicated if a person or public body would otherwise have an ability to appeal the decision of the Township of Centre Wellington to the Ontario Land Tribunal (OLT) but the person or public body does not make oral submissions at a public meeting or make written submissions to the Township of Centre Wellington before the by-law is passed, the person or public body is not entitled to appeal the decision.

Mayor Watters stated if a person or public body does not make oral submission at the public meeting, or make written submissions to the Township of Centre Wellington before the by-law is passed, the person or public body may not be added as the party to the hearing of an appeal before the OLT unless, in the opinion of the Tribunal, there are reasonable grounds to do so.

Mayor Watters advised if anyone wished to be notified of the adoption of the proposed zoning by-law amendment, a written request must be filed with the Municipal Clerk, Township of Centre Wellington, 1 MacDonald Square, Elora, ON, N0B 1S0.
The Municipal Clerk advised notice was provided to the prescribed persons, agencies and public bodies on or before February 26th, 2026.
A copy was also advertised in the Wellington Advertiser on February 26th, 2026. She further confirmed the requirement for giving notice was completed on February 26th, 2026.
Mayor Watters asked Mariana Iglesias, Manager of Planning Services, to introduce the application.

M. Iglesias stated the public meeting is regarding the zoning by-law amendment for short term rental accommodations and for Bed & Breakfast establishments; staff was directed by Council to draft a zoning by-law amendment as a supporting tool for the proposed licensing by- law for Short Term Rental Accommodations and Bed & Breakfasts.

She indicated the proposed zoning by-law concerns land use and how that land use is regulated. The draft zoning by-law is intended to provide clarity, outline the proposed changes to the regulations and provide an enforcement tool to assist with the implementation of a short-term rental licencing by-law.
Anthea Fisher, a resident of Elora residing in the C1 Zone, spoke in opposition to the proposed elimination of short-term rental units above commercial uses in the C1 Zone.

Ms. Fisher raised concerns regarding the parking requirements for short-term rentals, specifically the requirement that parking be located on an owned lot within 300 metres of the property. She noted this requirement is costly and difficult for property owners to achieve, particularly in the downtown core. As a result, the regulation would significantly reduce the number of short-term rental units and may incentivize an increase in hotel development in the downtown area.

She expressed concern with the proposed cap on short-term rentals, particularly, changes to the definition of “short-term rental” and the revised definition of “hotel.” She stated redefining hotels could result in a loss of long-term rental housing, as units may be converted to a hotel use while still falling outside the short-term rental cap.

Ms. Fisher encouraged Council to consider alternative approaches to securing parking, rather than imposing strict ownership-based requirements. She also expressed concern regarding a lack of transparency in the process, noting the implications of the proposed changes were not clearly communicated to affected property owners.

Darcy Saunders, resident, raised concerns regarding clarity and enforcement. He questioned whether the definitions and regulations would be applied and enforced consistently, the By-law defines a Bed & Breakfast as a property where the owner resides and requires one parking space per guest.

He expressed concern regarding consistency and fairness, noting that while one property is currently operating, another property is required to meet a higher threshold and emphasized the importance of regulations being applied consistently, transparently, and equitably across the Township.

Erika Montero, resident stated she supports the regulation of short-term rentals; however, she expressed opposition to the proposed zoning by- law amendment. She advised the proposed definition of “hotel,” described as a building or group of buildings, is overly broad and would be ineffective as an enforcement tool. She indicated the proposed definition could enable developers to avoid permitting requirements by converting short-term rental units into hotel-style accommodations.

She expressed concerns regarding the potential impact on the housing supply, noting zoning by-laws should protect residential housing and the proposed amendment would remove dwellings from the housing stock.

She further identified public safety concerns, stating hotels permitted through the zoning amendment would not be subject to the same safety regulations as short-term rentals and recommended restoring and strengthening the definition of “hotel” to ensure housing protection and public safety, emphasizing the importance of fairness and transparency in zoning regulations.
Sophie Hogan – did not attend.
Mayor Watters asked if anyone if anyone is present wished to speak to the application.

Glen Rumble, resident, expressed concerns about the proposed cap of 265 short-term rental units, stating it would reduce income opportunities for local homeowners. He commented the proposed zoning framework would heavily regulate short-term rentals under the new amendment.

He noted the most significant impacts of the proposed changes relate to the licensing constraints, which he indicated would be the most relevant and restrictive aspect of the by-law for property owners operating Bed & Breakfasts.
Mayor Watters asked Mariana Iglesias to respond to
comments/questions from council.

M. Iglesias addressed the issue of legal non-compliance and the change to the hotel definition. She noted when a unit is converted to an overnight accommodation for stays of less than 28 days, it is considered a hotel, as it constitutes a commercial use. As a hotel, the use had already undergone zoning and parking review at the time it was established. Therefore, additional parking requirements do not apply, since parking was addressed when the commercial use was originally reviewed.

M. Iglesias responded to questions from Council regarding the demerit point system and clarified that the demerit point system does not apply to hotels. Hotels are inspected for compliance with the Building Code at the time they are established. She further noted short term rentals are subject to parking requirements, which differ from those applicable to hotels.

B. Salmon clarified the purpose of the hotel definition, noting in the draft licencing by-law, the direction given by Council was to permit one (1) licence per property which impacted the properties located in the downtown core that have more than one unit. He explained if the hotel definition applied, they would not be subject to that limitation, if kept as STR’s the licencing would render a number of existing units noncompliant.

M. Iglesias responded to questions from Council regarding legal nonconforming status for those establishments currently operating as a B&B, explaining, under the new licencing by-law if the owner resides on- site, it remains a B&B, however, if the owner resides outside the main dwelling, they could apply for a minor variance but would still be required to reside on the main property.

M. Iglesias indicated staff will take the feedback and comments received from the public and Members of Council and bring back a revised draft amendment together with the STR licensing by-law for Council’s consideration.
Mayor Watters thanked everyone for attending and advised Council will be considering the by-law at a future Council meeting and declared the meeting adjourned.
Council resumed 7:15pm

Joseph Puopolo, Polycorp requested Council receive the current Development Charges Background Study for information, extend the existing Development Charges By-law, and provide additional time for staff, Council, and stakeholders to review and address outstanding matters outlined in his submission, including benefit of infrastructure to existing residents, timing of South Fergus infrastructure, lands not contemplated in the study assumptions, lands with standing in under The Planning Act, market feasibility and infrastructure delivery risk, and Highway access management and highway-related works.

items.title: Joe Harris, Grand Highlands Home Builders’ Association re Agenda
notes: Item 12.2, Development Charges Background Study and By-law J. Harris commented the shared objective is to realize more sustainable housing and support the community’s long term growth.

He noted it is difficult for the developers to absorb the level of DC increases at this time, as the housing market has slowed building activity has declined, housing prices remain high, and jobs across the housing sector are disappearing.

J. Harris indicated his appreciation for the additional measures established to defer DCs, however given the current geopolitical and economic uncertainty, a noticeable slowdown in housing activity, and the approach of the 2026 municipal election cycle, he suggested it not the appropriate time to implement increases of this magnitude. He encouraged Council to consider implementing a DC by-law that meets the needs of the Township without risking project viability, delaying or cancelling planned developments and constraining the supply of new housing.

items.title: Darcy Saunders re Agenda Item 12.1, Economic Development and
notes: Tourism Municipal Service Corporation Update

Darcy Saunders, expressed concerns regarding the proposed model, focusing on its structure, funding, and overall justification. He noted this proposal represents the first time the public has been presented with a complete version of the model, including its governance structure, projected costs, and implementation details. He emphasized an initiative of this magnitude should demonstrate a clear and transparent progression in the public domain prior to reaching this stage. He raised concerns that residents are being asked to fund the creation of the model through taxpayer dollars, despite the fact that the Municipal Accommodation Tax (MAT) has not yet been implemented.

D. Saunders highlighted that while the projected cost of the model is approximately $800,000, only $410,000 is expected to be contributed to the Corporation, leaving a substantial funding gap to be covered through municipal taxes and Ontario Lottery and Gaming (OLG) funding. This structure results in a partially subsidized system.

He further noted that local business operators who benefit directly from tourism activity are not being required to contribute financially to the program, placing a disproportionate burden on residents. Referencing public survey results, Saunders stated residents are not asking for more tourism, but rather for better support and management of the tourism activity that already exists within the community and raised concerns regarding the independence of the consultant involved in developing the model, noting the consultant previously served as Mayor.

items.title: Consideration of Reports
Economic Development and Tourism Municipal Service Corporation
notes: Update
Report from D. Wilson, Chief Administrative Officer

Kelly Linton, Linton Consulting Servies gave a presentation on the Municipal Service Corporation (MSC), including the organizational design, the four-phased approach, the engagement strategy and summarized the implementation process.

D. Wilson, Chief Administrative Officer provided an overview of the extensive public engagement conducted, the development of the Business Case Study and the completion of the comprehensive process mapping exercise. He indicated the by-law to establish the governance and administration framework to collect, audit, enforce, and allocated revenues will be brought forward at a later date.
D. Wilson noted staff is recommending the following at this time, • MAT be implemented at a rate of 5% of the purchase price of transient accommodation;

• The MAT will be calculated on the base accommodation charge paid by guests, excluding HST and any refundable deposits and applies to stays of 28 consecutive days or fewer at eligible accommodation establishments; and
• There will be provisions for MAT collection processes, audits, enforcement, etc.
He outlined how the Township will support the MSC going forward and outlined the next steps.

D. Wilson responded to comments and questions regarding the public engagement process, the MSC budgeting process, the timeline for recruitment of an Executive Director and Board Members, and how the MSC will support tourism and economic development.

items.title: Development Charges Background Study and By-law
notes: Report from D. Wilson, Chief Administrative Officer

D. Wilson, Chief Administrative Officer provided an overview regarding the purpose of development charges (DC), the DC study timeline, the DC study exemptions/discounts, DC affordable housing rates, and other legislative changes. He outlined addendums 1 and 2 resulting in a decrease in calculated DC rates, the local service policy and the DC deferral policy.

D. Wilson reviewed the calculated DC rates, reflective of addendums 1 and 2 and outlined the developer/building questions and comments, including the productive changes. He outlined the options for Council’s consideration including a) partial DC exemption for medium and high density intensification, b) a 6 month DC rate freeze and c) a 2-stage DC rate increase (50% of the total rate increase effective October 1, 2026, 50% if the rate increase effective April 1, 2027) or a 1-stage DC rate increase.
B. Salmon, Managing Director of Planning and Development responded to questions regarding partial DC exemption for high density and noted four plex units are considered medium density.

D. Wilson responded to comments and questions regarding partial exemptions based on growth projections, tracking building permits and development applications to identify if the 6 month freeze accelerates applications.

Discussion ensued regarding housing intensification and consideration of a partial exemption for housing other than medium and high density, the impact of the partial exemptions, and the cost of growth.

In light of discussions and additional questions, D. Wilson indicated if it is Council’s intent to keep the 5 dwelling unit rule and remove reference to medium and high density in the draft by-law, Section 3.8 m (iii) and n (iii) requires amending.

B. Salmon suggested removing reference to 5 dwelling units and medium and high density in Section 3.8 of the by-law to include exemptions to all types of housing and responded to questions regarding changing 5 to 4 to include semi-detached dwellings.

In response to a question regarding amendments to the intensification exemptions, Daryl Abbs, Partner, Watson & Associates Economists Ltd., indicated The Development Charges Act permits future amendments to the by-law to lower the charges or expand the exemptions.

items.title: Update on Proposed Use of 965 Gartshore Farmhouse
notes: Report from A. Gilmore, Managing Director of Community Services Adam Gilmore gave an overview of the report, indicating construction of the new Operations Centre is well underway. He indicated while past discussions have focused on repurposing the Gartshore Farmhouse for community use, staff have recently considered the possibility of converting it for use as additional office space for Township staff in the Community Services Department. He noted this change in direction is motivated by the following factors:
There is often a higher level of upgrade needed when converting to a public use building, compared to an office space accessed by employees only;
Direction from Township Council following Report No. CS2025-32:

Priority Setting for Indoor Recreation Facilities in September 2025 was to prioritize the construction of a new Multi-Use Recreation Facility (MURF), and construction of the MURF presents new opportunities to include community-use facilities at the Sportsplex site.

Adam Gilmore responded to comments and questions regarding the heritage value of the farmhouse, preservation of the exterior of the farmhouse building and modifications to the interior of the building, and possible use by community gardens groups for storage.
